sentences.text: After filing his appearance, the appellant appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of the PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analyzed from the Central Food Laboratory.
Application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave certificate dated 02.12.2008 opining the sample to be in contravention of Rules 29 of the PFA Rules, due to presence of synthetic food colour "Tartrazine".

5. Thereafter matter was listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 Sh. V.P.S. Chaudhary, Food Inspector, PW-2 Jagdish Prasad, FA and PW-3 Sh. Radha Charan he then SDM/LHA.
6.

On the basis of testimony of PW-1 Sh.V.P.S. Chaudhary, on 21.01.2010 charge was framed against the accused for commission of offences punishable u/s 7/16(1A) of PFA Act for violation of provisions of Sub clause (a)(j) and(m)of Section 2(ia) of PFA Act alleging therein that on 23.05.2008 at about 05.30 p.m, appellant being the Vendor cum Proprietor of M/s Sanjay Namkeen, E-1, East Vinod Nagar, Delhi 91 sold Namkeen for analysis, the sample consisted of approximately 900 grams taken from open polythene bag bearing no label declaration to F-1 Sh.
V.P.S. Chaduary in the presence of LHA and witness and the sample was analyzed by the CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 4 of 13 CFL vide Certificate no. CFL/389/574/2008 on 02.12.2008

and found that the sample contain synthetic food colour i.e. Trartrazine and hence contravenes Rule 1955 thereby he violated the provisions of sub caluse (a)(j) and (m) of Section 2(ia) of PFA Act, 1954 violated the Rules 30 read with Rule 28 and 29 of PFA Act punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Section 7 of the PFA Act to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

6.1 During trial after the examination and detailed cross examination of three witnesses i.e. PW1 PW-1 Sh. V.P.S. Chaudhary, Food Inspector, PW-2 Jagdish Prasad, FA and PW-3 Sh. Radha Charan he then SDM/LHA, prosecution evidence was closed and matter was fixed for Statement of accused .

7. The statement of accused was recorded under section 313 Cr.PC in which accused pleaded his innocence and admitted the sample proceedings dated 23.05.2008, yet he claimed that no efforts were made to join public witnesses ; stated that the sample was not taken properly as the sample bottles was not made clean and dry at the spot ; no adulteration was made by him ; expressed his intention to lead evidence in defence but no such evidence was led by him.

7.1 After hearing the arguments of both the parties, appellant was convicted by the learned trial court for commission of offence punishable under section punishable u/s 7/16(1A) PFA Act for violation of Section 2(ia)(a)
(j) and (m) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Rules 23,28,29 and 30 of PFA Rules.

8. The learned trial court in its impugned judgment dated 08.07.2016 observed that the samples had been collected according CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA)
Pages 5 of 13 to the prescribed procedures from the vendor cum Proprietor/ appellant premises, on analyzing the sample, it was opined vide PA report that the food sample is adulterated, appellant had sold adulterated food in violation of Section 2(ia)(a) (j) and ( m) of PFA Act and has committed the offence punishable u/s 7/16(1A) PFA Act.

sentences.text: 9.(I) The appellant has assailed the judgment and order on sentence passed by the learned trial court by urging various grounds.

II) Alternatively, on the quantum of sentence, relying upon the new legislation, it was pleaded that the case of the appellant be considered sympathetically in the light of the preposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Courts pursuant to coming of new legislation that is Food Safety & Standards Act.

10. During the course of argument on 09.10.2020, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that he is not challenging the merits of the case/ conviction decided by the learned trial court vide judgment dated 08.07.2016 and confining his appeal limited to the quantum of sentence only awarded to him vide order dated 13.07.2016 ; and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him by giving him the benefit of New Legislation as FSSAI.
11.

Learned counsel for the Delhi Admn./Food Department, objected to the same and submitted that according to statement of CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA)
Pages 6 of 13 appellant, prosecution has established its case and he be sentenced with strict punishment in terms of old Act wherein minimum punishment is prescribed and no leniency be shown to the convict as it is a serious offence of adulteration of food article / commodity leading to hazardous consequence to health and body of a person.
12.

sentences.text: I have carefully gone through the available record as well as trial court record, have heard the submissions of learned counsel for both the parties at length and have also gone through the judgments relied upon by the parties.

13. In light of above submissions and discussion particularly when the statement of appellant is recorded, I find no valid and legal reasons to interfere with the well reasoned judgment of the learned trial court.

The findings of the learned trial court with respect to the conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable under 16(1A) of the PFA Act read with Section 7 of the PFA Act,
1954 are upheld.
II. Now Coming to the alternate plea of giving benefit of new legislation to the appellant/ accused.
14. It is argued by learned counsel for the appellant that on the date of pronouncement of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed and new act had come into operation.

It is stated that the court should give benefit of the new legislation to the accused vide which the punishment provided under the old act has been diluted to a considerable extent, and that the offence for which the accused/appellant has been convicted now falls under the category of Unsafe Food punishable under section 59(1) of the new Act i.e Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 7 of 13 FSSA) punishable upto six months and fine of Rs. 1 lacs only.

It was argued by learned counsel for the appellant that appellant is a man of old age of 65 years,
respectable person of society, has deep roots in the society, has responsibility towards his family consisting of wife and children, is a small shop keeper, has problem in leg, unable to walk properly,
not keeping good health, not involved in any other case, the sample bottle was not made clean and dry at the spot; and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him in light of the provisions of law under the new Act.

15.1 Further that the case pertains to the year 2008, the appellant/accused has faced the trial almost 12 years which by itself is a sufficient punishment and the hardships faced by him caused him great mental agony, stress and rigors of trial during the said period.

It is also stated that now a days special circumstances exists due to outbreak of pandemic of Covid-19 and there are chances of appellant being infected with virus in case imprisonment of sentence is awarded to him.

15.2 In support of his submissions, learned counsel for appellant had relied upon the judgment of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203 ) of Hon'ble Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai Vs. Henry 1983 ( ) SCC 177. 15.3 Per contra, learned SPP, strongly opposed the submissions advanced by learned counsel by addressing that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences are CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 8 of 13 changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.

sentences.text:
Definition of major offences like "adulteration"
and "misbranding" have been changed.
Now FSSA have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter" "unsafe food" and misbranded food".
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.
15.4 As far as the objection of learned SPP is concerned, in the present case, the offence was that the article/food was found adulterated and was unfit for human consumption.

This was violation of Rules under PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Section 2(1a)(a) (j) & (m) of the PFA Act and thus consequently punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act read with Section 7 of PFA Act.
15.5 That now in the FSSA such adulteration is termed as "unsafe food" in terms of Section 3(zz)(viii) of FSSA Act and violation thereof is punishable u/s 59(1) of FSSA.
So if we go through both these provisions of law a particular offence with a particular fact is mentioned with some other name but with same ingredients in the New FSSA Act.

- Sub-clause (viii) of 3(zz) FSSA Act is applicable where the colouring material or the preservative other than that specified in respect there of is found in the food article and no where the colouring material exceeds the prescribed limit.

15.6 Further, the charge in this case was framed for the said offences and there is no charge in which it is stated that the said CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 9 of 13 colour was injuries to health.

Therefore, it is held that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence determines that whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence, Here the offence of adding colour in the food article which was punishable u/s 16(1)(a) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/s Raja Ram Rathore vs Delhi Administration/ on 14 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/127643620/
5 59(1) of FSSA Act, which is now punishable with simple imprisonment of six months and fine upto one lac only.

sentences.text: 15.8 As far as the application of Nemi Chand Judgment (supra) is concerned, the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T Barai ( Supra) of Hon'ble Supreme Court.

The relevant portion of the T Barai Judgment is as follows :
- (Para 25) It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication in Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80 Lord Campbell put the matter thus :
- "It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an ofence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute see also Smith Vs.
Benabo ( 1937) 1 ALL ER 523 : ( 1997) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194"
- In Regina Vs. Youle ( 1861) 158 ER 311,315-16 : LT 299 : 9 WR 637 Martin B. said in the oft-quoted passage :
CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 10 of 13 - If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offence, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."

sentences.text: - The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.

- Moreover, this particular aspect is stated as a illustration in the same judgment in Para 23 which is as follows :
- To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life, then it can not be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.

sentences.text: - In view of the above mentioned discussion, it can be safely said that while considering on the point of sentence, the quantum of sentence in new Act i.e. FSSA is to be considered.

16. Thus analysing the facts of the case, taking note of the special circumstances of the case concerning the accused and the fact that accused has faced the trial of almost 12 years ; and also the fact that extraordinary circumstances exists due to outbreak of Covid 19 ; and in light of the above cited judgment and the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi titled as GNCT Vs. Jagdish Tyagi dated 11.10.2017 in my view the convict/ appellant is entitled to the benefit of new legislation.

Accordingly to meet the ends of justice, the sentence of the convict Raja Ram Rathore as imposed by the learned trial court vide order dated 13.07.2016 stands modified to the extent that the order sentencing the appellant to undergo simple imprisonment of two years stands waived of to simple imprisonment for one day i.e. till rising of the court ; the sentence of fine is enhanced from Rs.
50,000/- to Rs. 1,00,000/-
In default of payment of fine the appellant/convict shall undergo simple imprisonment for two months.
Senence modified accordingly.

17 Appellant/Convict is directed to deposit the fine amount within 30 days from the date of pronouncement of this judgment before the learned trial court and, if any, amount of fine was deposited by the appellant before the learned trial court same shall be adjusted accordingly.
18. The present appeal is disposed of accordingly in terms CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 12 of 13 thereof.

1.
For the reasons stated in the application, 90 days' delay in filing the appeal is condoned.
2. Application is disposed of.
1. State is in appeal feeling aggrieved by the judgment dated 24th November, 2016 and the sentence awarded to the respondent by learned ASJ-01 while disposing of Criminal Appeal No.8550/2016.

Vide impugned judgment, the sentence awarded to the respondent by the learned ACMM in CC No.193/2012 has been reduced by the learned ASJ-01 as under:
Sentence awarded by ACMM Under Section 16(1A) r/w Section 7 In CC No.193/2002 of PFA Act, 1954 - to undergo SI for 18 months and fine of CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 16 of 13 `10,000/-.

sentences.text: In default SI for 60 days.
Sentence reduced by ASJ-01, Under Section 59(i) of FSSA - to New Delhi in CA undergo imprisonment till the rising No.8550/2016 of the Court and to pay a fine of `35,000/-.
In default to undergo SI for 15 days.
2. The respondent/accused has not challenged his conviction or the order on sentence.

The State is aggrieved to the limited extent that the respondent/accused could not have been awarded the sentence 'till rising of the Court' as the minimum sentence prescribed in the law is three months.

The grounds of challenge in appeal are as under:
"A. Because the impugned order is manifestly wrong, illegal and against the facts on record. B. Because the order of Ld. Appellate Court is against the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Criminal Appeal No.1570/2010 titled as Mithlesh Vs. State of NCT of Delhi wherein it was held that "no further benevolence can be shown to the appellant, more so, when it is a case of food adulteration.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
There is no special circumstance which may warrant reducing the sentence below the minimum"
C.
Because the Ld. Appellate Court failed to appreciate that the offence committed by the accused was serious in nature and hence the Ld.Trial Court had awarded him the sentence of 18 months.

D. Because the Ld.Appellate Court erred in reducing the sentence from 18 months, awarded by the Ld.Trial Court, to till the rising of the Court, as the minimum sentence prescribed in the law is three months.
E. Because the Ld.Appellate Court did not appreciate the legal position correctly.
F. That the petitioner craves leave to this Hon'ble Court to add, amend or drop any of the grounds.
G. That no such similar or other petition has been filed either before this Hon'ble Court or before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India."

sentences.text: learned ASJ has rightly held it to be an offence punishable under Section 59(i) of FSSA Act for the purpose of awarding the punishment and no minimum sentence is prescribed for the above said offence.

5. Learned APP for the State fairly concedes that in the grounds of appeal there is no challenge to the finding of the learned ASJ that Dal Arhar coloured with synthetic colour "Tartrazine" is termed as "unsafe food" in terms of Sec.3(zz) (vii) of FSSA Act punishable under Section 59(i) of FSSA and no minimum sentence is prescribed there under.

6. Learned ASJ considered that since on the date of judgment and order on sentence in this case, the PFA Act, 1954 stood repealed, the learned Trial Court should have passed the order on sentence as per provisions of Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA) as held in Nemi Chand's case (supra).

The reasons given for awarding the sentence till rising of the Court but enhancing the quantum of fine are as under:-
"14.
As far as the objection of Ld.SPP for State is concerned, in the present case, the offence was that the article/food ie. Dal Arhar was foud as being coloured with synthetic colour "Tartrazine".
This was violation of Rule 29 of PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Section.2(ia)(i) of PFA Act and thus consequently punishable u/sec.16(1) of PFA Act.
The charge was framed with these facts.
There was no charge in which it is stated that the said colour was injurious to health.
Had it been the case, the charge should have been u/sec.16(1-A) (ii) of PFA Act.

15. Now in the FSSA, such adulteration is termed as "unsafe food"
in terms of Sec.3(zz) (vii) of FSSA Act punishable u/sec.59(i) of FSSA.
16.
Hence, it is held that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence, determines that whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence.
Here the offence of adding colour in the food article which was punishable u/sec.16(1A) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/sec.59(i) of FSSA Act."

7. After placing reliance on the decision of the Supreme Court in Nemi Chand's case (supra), the learned ASJ arrived at the conclusion that adding colour to the food article i.e. Dal Arhar in the instant case, which was earlier punishable under Section 16(1A) of PFA Act has to be considered an Raja Ram Rathore vs Delhi Administration/ on 14 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/127643620/

opennyai_summary.facts:
By way of present appeal, the appellant Raja Ram Rathore herein has challenged the judgment dated 08.07.2016 and order on the point of sentence dated 13.07.2016 passed by the then learned ACMM-II, PHC, New Delhi vide which the appellant/accused was held guilty for commission of offences punishable under sections 16(1A) r/w Section 7 of PFA Act, 1954, the appellant was awarded a sentence to undergo Simple Imprisonment for 02 years as well as to pay fine of Rs.50,000/- for commission of aforesaid offences and in dafault of payment of fine to undergo Simple Imprisonment of 15 days.
3. The brief facts of the present case are that on 23.05.2008, the Food Inspector Sh. V.P.S.
Chaudhary, Food Assistant Sh. Jagdish Prasad, under the supervision of Local Health Authority/SDM Sh. Radha Charan reached at the premises of M/s Sanjay Namkeet at E-1, East Vinod Nagar, Delhi, where accused CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 2 of 13 /appellant was found conducting his business of various food articles/Namkeen which were lying stored in an open polythene bag without label or declaration meant for sale for human consumption ;
- that FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Namkeen' from the vendor which was lying in open gunny bag bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed ;
- that thereafter as per the prescribed procedure under the PFA Act and Rules after giving notice to the vendor/appellant and offer towards sale price of sample to which he agreed and accept, sample was then lifted ; that sample was separately packed, fastened, marked, sealed and necessary documents including Notice as per Form-VI in the presence of appellant/accused, panchnama etc was prepared at the spot ; that thereafter one counterpart of sample was sent to Public Analyst (PA)
in intact condition and other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA ;
- that vide report dated 06.06.2008, PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that total dye content of synthetic colour used "Tartrazine and Brilliant Blue FCF" was 630.56 ppm which wasin excess of the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm;
- that upon receipt of report, SDM/LHA directed investigation which was carried out by FI and after completion of investigation sanction under Section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 25.09.2008 alleging violation of Section 2(ia)(a),(j) and (m) of PFA Act, read with Rules 28,29 and 30 of PFA Rules as punishable under Section 7/16(1)(A) of PFA. Act.
CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 3 of 13 - that the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, hence, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with ;
4.
After filing his appearance, the appellant appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of the PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analyzed from the Central Food Laboratory.
The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave certificate dated 02.12.2008 opining the sample to be in contravention of Rules 29 of the PFA Rules, due to presence of synthetic food colour "Tartrazine".
On the basis of testimony of PW-1 Sh.V.P.S. Chaudhary, on 21.01.2010 charge was framed against the accused for commission of offences punishable u/s 7/16(1A) of PFA Act for violation of provisions of Sub clause (a)(j) and(m)of Section 2(ia) of PFA Act alleging therein that on 23.05.2008 at about 05.30 p.m, appellant being the Vendor cum Proprietor of M/s Sanjay Namkeen, E-1, East Vinod Nagar, Delhi 91 sold Namkeen for analysis, the sample consisted of approximately 900 grams taken from open polythene bag bearing no label declaration to F-1 Sh.
V.P.S. Chaduary in the presence of LHA and witness and the sample was analyzed by the CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 4 of 13 CFL vide Certificate no. CFL/389/574/2008 on 02.12.2008
and found that the sample contain synthetic food colour i.e. Trartrazine and hence contravenes Rule 1955 thereby he violated the provisions of sub caluse (a)(j) and (m) of Section 2(ia) of PFA Act, 1954 violated the Rules 30 read with Rule 28 and 29 of PFA Act punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Section 7 of the PFA Act to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
7.1 After hearing the arguments of both the parties, appellant was convicted by the learned trial court for commission of offence punishable under section punishable u/s 7/16(1A) PFA Act for violation of Section 2(ia)(a)
(j) and (m) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Rules 23,28,29 and 30 of PFA Rules.
The appellant was accordingly convicted and sentenced by the learned trial court and aggrieved by the said judgment and order on quantum of Raja Ram Rathore vs Delhi Administration/ on 14 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/127643620/
3 sentence dated 13.07.2016, the present appeal has been preferred by the appellant.
The State is aggrieved to the limited extent that the respondent/accused could not have been awarded the sentence 'till rising of the Court' as the minimum sentence prescribed in the law is three months.
D. Because the Ld.Appellate Court erred in reducing the sentence from 18 months, awarded by the Ld.Trial Court, to till the rising of the Court, as the minimum sentence prescribed in the law is three months.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
II) Alternatively, on the quantum of sentence, relying upon the new legislation, it was pleaded that the case of the appellant be considered sympathetically in the light of the preposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Courts pursuant to coming of new legislation that is Food Safety & Standards Act.
It is stated that the court should give benefit of the new legislation to the accused vide which the punishment provided under the old act has been diluted to a considerable extent, and that the offence for which the accused/appellant has been convicted now falls under the category of Unsafe Food punishable under section 59(1) of the new Act i.e Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 7 of 13 FSSA) punishable upto six months and fine of Rs. 1 lacs only.
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.
Learned APP for the State submitted that in decision reported as Mithlesh vs. State of NCT of Delhi (2014) 123 SCC 423, the Apex Court refused to further reduce the sentence observing that it was a case of food adulteration and there was no special circumstance warranting reducing the sentence below the minimum, especially when the High Court had already shown benevolence by reducing the sentence from one year to three months.
4. Mr.K.K.Manan, Learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent has submitted that the case of the respondent is squarely covered by this recent decision of the Supreme Court in the case Nemi CA no.8726/16 Raja Ram Rathore Vs.Delhi Admn/Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 17 of 13 Chand vs. State of Rajasthan II (2016) CCR 15 (SC).
learned ASJ has rightly held it to be an offence punishable under Section 59(i) of FSSA Act for the purpose of awarding the punishment and no minimum sentence is prescribed for the above said offence.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
This was violation of Rules under PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Section 2(1a)(a) (j) & (m) of the PFA Act and thus consequently punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act read with Section 7 of PFA Act.
7. After placing reliance on the decision of the Supreme Court in Nemi Chand's case (supra), the learned ASJ arrived at the conclusion that adding colour to the food article i.e. Dal Arhar in the instant case, which was earlier punishable under Section 16(1A) of PFA Act has to be considered an Raja Ram Rathore vs Delhi Administration/ on 14 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/127643620/
Since no minimum sentence is prescribed under Section 59(i) of FSSA, the findings given by learned ASJ and sentence awarded to the appellant, therefore, cannot be faulted.
